title: TB8-33187
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): The principal Appellant XXXX XXXX and her minor son XXXX XXXX (the minor Appellant), both citizens of Iran, are appealing a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) refusing their claims for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: The principal Appellant XXXX XXXX and her minor son XXXX XXXX (the minor Appellant), both citizens of Iran, are appealing a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) refusing their claims for refugee protection.
For the following reasons, I dismiss this appeal. BACKGROUND OF APPEAL The Appellants' claims, the RPD's decision, and the Appellants' arguments before the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD)

Before the RPD the Appellants alleged they faced a serious forward-looking risk of persecution in their native Iran on the grounds of religion and imputed political opinion. The minor Appellant's claim was based on his mother's claim. The RPD refused the claims on the grounds of credibility. The RPD observed that there was "no evidence in this claim in regard to the events that supposedly occurred in Iran", and that it did not accept the principal Appellant's "allegations in regard to the ... [Appellants'] religious conversion".1

Notably, the RPD found "[t]here were striking similarities between the ... [Appellants'] allegations and those contained in another Iranian Christian convert case, file TB7-22807."2 It rejected the principal Appellant's explanation for the similarities and found "that some third party has been orchestrating both sets of claimants' activities in Canada and coaching them" in both their respective claims.3

Before the RAD the Appellants submit the RPD violated their right to procedural fairness by "disclosing only part of the [separate and distinct] refugee claim in [RPD file number] TB7-22807", specifically by "failing to disclose that TB7-22807 was rejected for reasons independent of the similarities, and in failing to give the Appellants notice that the RPD thought a third party orchestrated [both] the refugee claims."4

The Appellants submit also that the RPD erred: - in finding that their refugee claims were orchestrated by a third party and in rejecting their explanations for similarities in their claims and the claims in RPD case TB7-22807;5 - by not giving enough weight to the testimony of their pastor who testified at their hearing;6 - in finding there was no evidence the Appellants' activities would come to the attention of authorities in Iran;7 - in law by applying the wrong standard of proof to that aspect of their claims that arose in Canada (their sur place claims);8 and - by failing to independently assess whether the minor Appellant's conversion to Christianity was genuine.9 NEW EVIDENCE & REQUEST FOR AN ORAL HEARING Decision on Appellants' new evidence applications

The Appellants have asked to admit the following documents as new evidence in this appeal: - Subject to subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA),10 the affidavit of XXXX (a.k.a. XXXX) XXXX dated XXXX XXXX, 201911 ("the XXXX Affidavit"); and - Subject to rule 29 of the Refugee Appeal Division Rules,12 (1) further submissions in an application dated March 21, 2019,13 (2) an affidavit and photographs and letters in an application dated September 16, 2019,14 (3) an affidavit and letter in an application received by the Board's Registry on January 23, 2020 and dated January 22, 2020,15 and (4) an affidavit and letter in an application dated August 19, 2020.

Rule 29 allows for the submission of documents and/or written submissions not previously provided in an appellant's record, subject to certain criteria. A rule 29 application must include "an explanation of how the document meets the requirements of subsection 110(4) of the Act [IRPA] and how that evidence relates to the person".16 For its part, subsection 110(4) of the IRPA17 states I can only accept as new evidence documents that: i. arose after the RPD decision; or ii. were not reasonably available at the time of the decision; or iii. the appellant could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to bring to the RPD before the decision.
If an item meets one or more of these requirements, before I can accept it I must consider whether it is new, credible and relevant.18

I am satisfied that each of the Appellants' four rule 29 applications meets the requirements of rule 29(3) of the Refugee Appeal Division Rules: - The application of March 21, 2019 explains the Appellants wish to make further submissions on the impact of a decision made by the RAD in file number TB7-16268 that was designated a persuasive decision on February 27, 2019, after the Appellants perfected their appeal on January 14, 2019.19 - The application of September 16, 2019 explains that the evidence "relates to events that have transpired after the [Appellants'] Record" was perfected and dates from January 2019 to the date of the application, showing "the Appellants have continued to attend the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and openly practice their faith in that environment."20 It also explains the enclosed letter from XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX dated XXXX XXXX, 2019 "was also not available at the time the Record was perfected because he joined the Church as lead pastor only in XXXX-2019."21 - The application of January 22, 2020 explains that the letter it discloses is intended to correct a letter disclosed in the rule 29 application of September 16, 2019 and confirms that the evidence concerns events that post-date the RPD's determination.22 - Likewise, the application of August 19, 2020 explains that the evidence attached to it "relates to events that have transpired after the Record was perfected in this matter and after the previous Rule 29 Application" and discusses "the Appellants' religious faith and activities during the time since the prior letter, and in particular during the time of the COVID-19 pandemic and its related restrictions."23
The Appellants' further submissions of March 21, 2019 meet the explicit statutory requirements of subsection 110(4) of the IRPA as they post-date the RPD's refusal of the Appellants' claims.

Similarly, all of the exhibits to the affidavit of the principal Appellant in the September 16, 2019 rule 29 application record post-date the RPD's determination, as does the letter of XXXX XXXX dated XXXX XXXX, 2020 in the January 22, 2020 rule 29 application record and XXXX XXXX second letter dated XXXX XXXX, 2020 in the August 19, 2020 rule 29 application record.

The credibility of these documents, including the submissions, is not in issue, and their content is novel and directly relevant to my assessment of issues raised by the Appellants in this appeal. I therefore admit the rule 29 documents and will consider them alongside the submissions in the Appellants' record.

Concerning the application under subsection 110(4) of the IRPA, the XXXX Affidavit meets the explicit statutory requirements of this provision as it post-dates the RPD's refusal of the Appellants' claims. The affidavit is credible at first glance. Although its content is not novel, in the sense that it pre-dates the RPD's determination of the Appellants' claims, it is relevant to my assessment of issues raised by the Appellants in this appeal. I therefore admit the XXXX Affidavit into evidence. Decision on Appellants' request for an oral hearing

The Appellants have asked me to convene an oral hearing in accordance with subsection 110(6) of the IRPA. If there is new evidence in an appeal, the RAD may hold a hearing if that new evidence raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the appellant, is central to the RPD decision, and that, if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim.24

While I have considered paragraphs 80 to 85 of the Appellants' written submissions in their record of January 14, 2019,25 having read the new evidence I find it does not raise any serious issues with the Appellants' credibility.
I therefore decline to hold an oral hearing in this matter.

My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.26 I will apply the correctness standard of review after independently assessing the record in order to determine whether the RPD erred. I will only show deference to the RPD's credibility assessment and/or to its weighing of the oral evidence in situations where the RPD enjoys a particular advantage. If I find the RPD had a particular advantage, my reasons will explain why.

My determination is based on my independent assessment of the evidence before me. This includes: the records prepared by the RPD and the Appellants, including the Appellants' rule 29 records of March 21, 2019, September 16, 2019, January 22, 2020 and August 19, 2020 and the submissions therein; audio recordings of both sittings of the Appellants' RPD hearing on June 8, 2018 and November 22, 2018; transcripts of both sittings of the RPD hearing; and documents contained in the current compilation of the National Documentation Package (NDP) for Iran. Preliminary Issue: alleged breach of procedural fairness

The Appellants submit the RPD violated their right to procedural fairness by "failing to disclose that TB7-22807 was rejected for reasons independent of the similarities, and in failing to give the Appellants notice that the RPD thought a third party orchestrated the [two] refugee claims."27

In my independent assessment the Appellants' argument is not supported by the evidence. I have reviewed both sittings of the Appellants' RPD hearing. In the first sitting of the hearing on June 8, 2018 the RPD explained its decision to adjourn the proceedings to a new date: Madam, we will need to stop today. And this -- I will try to explain it as best I can to you. You've said a few things today in your testimony that have triggered some things for me. And I have noticed other things in your file that would influence my decision making. And in fairness to you, you should be made known of what knowledge I have. And in fairness to you, you should be given the opportunity to respond to those concerns. Okay. This must sound very mysterious, but I'm not able to say much more than that for privacy reasons. And I will have to follow a procedure under Rule 21 of our rules before I can properly disclose this information to you. Okay. But since I do have this knowledge that I can't share with you at this point in time, it would not be proper for us to continue this hearing today. Okay. So we will have to schedule a new hearing date for you, and we will have to disclose information to you after we follow our Rule 21 procedure. Okay. Counsel, I'm afraid I can't say very much more than that.28

At the start of the second sitting on November 22, 2018 the RPD panel stated: ... We did hear quite a bit of testimony from you at the last hearing. We were talking about your church activities in Canada and some of your testimony gave me some concern at the time. But for privacy reasons, I was not able to disclose what those concerns were. And this led to us scheduling another hearing date for you. And after your first hearing, a Rule 21, well, we call it a Rule 21 request. Essentially what 15 that does is it takes evidence from another file at our Board, and discloses it into your own claim. And it's administratively somewhat of a lengthy process because we take into account the views of the people who are concerned in the other file and we do have to conduct a risk assessment. And in this particular case, a number of documents were sent out to you to be entered as evidence. And this includes another -- this includes a page from the Basis of Claim form from another file. One of the names has not been redacted on that page. There's also birth certificates from the other file that have been disclosed. As well as church letters, a photograph, and, finally, a partial transcript from the hearing of that claim.29

The RPD panel and the Appellants' then counsel had the following exchange concerning the limits of the panel's ability to disclose information from the file in case TB7-22807 in the Appellants' RPD proceeding: MEMBER: Okay. There were some concerns from the claimant in the other file that was subject to the Rule 21 disclosure, and there are some boundaries that we've set around privacy for that. So I'm going to make sure that I don't overstep in the questions to him. But he may voluntarily disclose things that I'm not supposed to disclose, at least. COUNSEL: Can you tell us what kinds of things you're not to disclose because of the concerns? MEMBER: I think it would be difficult to describe them to you without breaching the privacy of the other --- COUNSEL: Sure. MEMBER: --- claimant. COUNSEL: Okay. MEMBER: Okay. But certainly, counsel, if there's any objections to any of the questions to the witness, please bring them to my attention as they arise. COUNSEL: Are the boundaries that have been set with respect to information the Board can disclose about the other claimant or are you -- are there boundaries with respect to what you can ask? I'm not clear on that. MEMBER: So there's boundaries around what I can disclose through my questions. COUNSEL: Okay. MEMBER: But I suppose if the pastor voluntarily raises them on his own and brings that information to light, that will be his voluntary disclosure. I just have to be careful not to have that come out involuntarily.30

First, the RPD took great effort to explain to the Appellants and their counsel that despite the Rule 21 disclosure it was required to protect the privacy of the claimants in TB7-22807. To that end it disclosed only as much information from the claims in TB7-22807 as was necessary to address concerns it had about similarities between the evidence in that case and the Appellants' case. My review of the record has not brought up any indication the RPD failed to disclose relevant information from TB7-22807-that is, the RPD reasons do not refer to information from that case that was not disclosed to the Appellants on either April 23, 2018 or August 8, 2018.

The above excerpts from the transcripts of both sittings show the RPD clearly explained that it was prevented from disclosing further details in order to protect the privacy of the claimants in TB7-22807. This was a valid reason for constraining the disclosure of information from that case to the Appellants to only that material that gave rise to the concerns about similar evidence that the RPD explained to the principal Appellant near the start of the second sitting.31

Second, the record of disclosures shows there is no merit to the Appellants' submission that they were "forced to operate in the blind" in addressing the RPD panel's concerns.32 The first package of information from case TB7-22807 was disclosed on April 23, 2018, several months before the first sitting of the Appellants' hearing on June 8, 2018. The second package of information from TB7-22807 was disclosed to the Appellants on August 8, 2018, 21 days before the next scheduled sitting of the hearing before the RPD on August 29, 2018. The record does not show that relevant information from TB7-22807 was either (a) withheld from the Appellants or (b) not disclosed to them in a timely fashion.

Third, the reasons for decision in TB7-22807 are confidential and the RPD was not required to disclose them to the Appellants, as rule 21(1) of the Refugee Protection Division Rules states that the panel "may disclose to a claimant personal and other information that it wants to use from any other claim",33 not that it must or even may disclose final reasons for decision in matters to which a claimant is not party. Indeed, as the RPD explained, privacy considerations prevented it from doing so.

Fourth, the Appellants have not explained how they "would have been able to use" the reasons for decision in TB7-22807 "to further argue that they were the victim of a copy-cat claim and that no third party orchestrated their claim."34 Their submission that "TB7-22807 was rejected independent ... [of] any similarities" is pure speculation that does not support their assertion that "those claimants were not credible regarding ... [their] story and supports the view that they borrowed it from the Appellants."35

In my independent assessment, evidence disclosed from the claims in TB7-22807 suggests that the case and the Appellants' case relied so strongly on a near-identical fact pattern and evolved over so similar a timeline that it was open to the RPD to conclude that there was some element of fabrication, and to make specific findings only after it had considered the evidence. Because the panel's finding was made after it considered all the evidence and the Appellants' explanations, the fact "the Appellants were never advised during either hearing that the RPD was of the view that a third party orchestrated their claims"36 does not amount to deprivation of notice and does not give rise to a violation of the Appellants' right to procedural fairness.

The evidence before me indicates the RPD acted fairly in giving the Appellants a chance to respond to its concerns about the similarities in the two cases, and by entertaining the principal Appellant's explanations for the credibility issues the RPD raised. The RPD did not violate the Appellants' right to procedural fairness.

As I explain below it was open to the RPD to find the Appellants' credibility was undermined. Although the RPD erred in making a specific finding of third-party orchestration in the Appellants' claims and the claims in TB7-22807, in my independent assessment the principal Appellant's inability to explain the similarities between her claim and the claims in TB7-22807 is nonetheless a sufficient basis for a serious adverse credibility finding. The RPD's credibility assessment

The Appellants submit there is no evidence to support the RPD's findings "that the similarities between the claims were not merely coincidental" or "that both claims were fraudulently orchestrated by a third party".37 The Appellants give two reasons for asserting that the RPD erred in finding both cases were orchestrated by a third party: - First, they assert the similarities between the two cases is because "these incidents occurred around the same time" and both groups of claimants attended key events at St. Luke's Church in Canada concurrently because they had no choice but to follow the programming schedule set by the church;38 and - Second, they assert the RPD discussed irrelevant factors before concluding that a third party orchestrated both cases, such as whether Mr. XXXX XXXX approached the Appellants in the supermarket or approached them outside, or the dates of the respective legal aid applications of both parties.39

They assert the RPD overstated similarities between the two cases because it "erroneously relied on the evidence regarding the role of Mr. XXXX" in each of the two cases to conclude that both "were orchestrated by a third party".40 They submit "the claims in TB7-22807 were rejected for reasons unrelated to the similarities between the two claims" while the Appellants' own claims were "rejected only because of the similarities between the two files."41

The Appellants assert further that "the timing of the claims point[s] to TB7-22807 being a copy-cat claim"42 as those claims were filed with the RPD after the Appellants' claims. According to the Appellants "the only ... reasonable conclusion is that TB7-22807 was a copy-cat claim" that copied elements of their own claims.43

The Appellants submit the RPD should have decided whether to accept the Appellants' explanations for the similarities between the two cases only after hearing and considering "'any evidence the claimant brings to support the assertion that their story is authentic, including possibly elements from the narrative itself'", but that instead the RPD "rejected" their "reasonable explanations simply because it had concocted a speculative theory of its own to explain the relationship between the narratives."44

Based on my reading of the RPD Record, I do not agree that the RPD "significantly overstated" the similarities between the two cases,45 which are evident in both records and were not disputed by the Appellants or their then counsel.

Both the Appellants and the claimants in TB7-22807 asserted that the Sepah in Iran raided their respective homes on the very same date: XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017. When the RPD asked the principal Appellant about this similarity in the first sitting, she testified "Iran is a dangerous country and that kind of event or occurrence could occur anywhere at any time".46 I find her testimony failed to address with specificity the RPD's concern that the Sepah raid she alleged took place in Iran on XXXX XXXX, 2017 was concurrent with an alleged Sepah raid in Iran referenced in the TB7-22807 Basis of Claim form (BOC), a similarity the RPD outlined extensively during the sitting.47

In the second sitting the RPD set out further similarities between the Appellants' claims and the claims in TB7-22807: the circumstances in which they first met Mr. XXXX XXXX in Canada;48 the date on which they first attended XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX, 2017 and the timing as well as the dates of their participation in church events, including their baptism in XXXX 2018.49 The principal Appellant initially explained that she and her spouse and son did not come to Canada as tourists, and that "the incident which my sister-in-law mentioned [the Sepah raid of XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017] has happened".50

Shortly thereafter, however, when the RPD said that it was "trying to understand how these similarities could happen, so many of them, between yours [the principal Appellant's] and another claim", the principal Appellant responded "I don't know the reason why. I don't know."51 I find her response inadequate to address the specific concerns raised by the RPD. The principal Appellant was similarly unable to explain similarities in the timing of her own legal aid application and the legal aid application made by the claimants in TB7-22807.52

In my independent assessment, the proximity of the dates of the legal aid applications in the Appellants' claims and in TB7-22807 was not relevant to the RPD's assessment of the credibility of the substance of their claims, since their respective applications were separated by a few days.

I also find that the concurrent nature of the church events that took place in Canada after the Appellants and the claimants in TB7-22807 joined XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX could be explained logically with reference to the schedule of worship services and activities set by the church, a schedule over which the Appellants had no control.

As well, I find that since parties to both cases identified Mr. XXXX XXXX as the person who invited them to join the Iranian congregation at XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX after they came to Canada, and since parties to both cases attended their first service at the church on XXXX XXXX, 2017 it was open to the RPD to assess the relevancy of any similarities in the circumstances in which the Appellants and the claimants in TB7-22807 met Mr. XXXX.

In my independent assessment, the fact that many events in Iran and the first major event in Canada discussed in the BOCs of the Appellants and the claimants in TB7-22807 took place on exactly the same dates properly gave rise to concerns on the part of the RPD. I find that the RPD did not overstate the similarities between the Appellants' claims and the claims in TB7-22807.
I turn now to the Appellants' submission that "the only ... reasonable conclusion is that TB7-22807 was a copy-cat claim" that copied elements of their own claims.53

The RPD considered this possibility but was "not satisfied ... that this could reasonably explain the similarities" because the principal Appellant's account of meeting Mr. XXXX XXXX in an Iranian shopping plaza in Toronto did not appear in either her BOC or in the Farsi script she prepared in anticipation of writing her BOC narrative.54

This information did appear, however, in the BOC narrative in TB7-22807, and the claimants in that case gave testimony to that effect in their RPD hearing, which occurred on April 30, 2018, months before the sittings of the Appellants' hearings on June 8, 2018 and November 22, 2018.55

The Appellants submit they did not think the circumstances in which they met Mr. XXXX was "sufficiently important to include in her [the principal Appellant's] Farsi draft narrative".56 They also submit the mere fact their "encounter with Mr. XXXX was not included" in their BOC narrative or Farsi preparatory document does not mean the principal Appellant "was provided with this information by a third party subsequent to filing her claim."57

Having considered the evidence before me, I accept the Appellants' latter submission that the RPD's finding of third-party orchestration of the Appellants' claims and the claims in TB7-22807 was "speculative" and without adequate evidentiary foundation. In my independent assessment the RPD's particular finding that there was "a third party" that orchestrated similarities in the Appellants' claims and in the claims in TB7-22807 was essentially a plausibility finding that failed to identify with specificity who this third party or parties might be.

As I do not believe it was open to the RPD to make so specific a finding without identifying clearly and convincingly where and how certain parts of the evidentiary record support a finding of "third party" involvement, I find the RPD erred in making this specific finding.

At the same time, however, I reject the principal Appellant's submission that her encounter with MrXXXX XXXX XXXX in which he invited her to XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX was not important enough to mention in her BOC and Farsi preparatory document, since she mentioned that Mr. XXXX referred her to his church in the first sitting of her RPD hearing: MEMBER: Yes. Okay. Since you've come to Canada, it seems that you've joined a church. CLAIMANT: XXXX XXXX. MEMBER: What kind of church is this? CLAIMANT: Protestant. MEMBER: And why did you decide to join XXXX XXXX in particular? CLAIMANT: Because I heard that it had lots of members, Iranian members, and they were from my country. MEMBER: Okay. Did someone refer you to that church? CLAIMANT: Yeah, through a friend. MEMBER: Which friend? CLAIMANT: Mr. XXXX XXXX (Ph.). May I expand on that? MEMBER: Yes.58

Considering the role that Mr. XXXX played in introducing both the Appellants and the claimants in TB7-22807 to XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, the site of much of their religious activity in Canada, the fact the Appellants likely knew him by the time they made refugee claims was relevant to the RPD's credibility assessment, when all the similarities between the two cases are considered cumulatively.

Finally, in their further submissions of March 21, 2019 the Appellants submit the RPD's reasoning concerning their credibility is contrary to the framework of analysis in the reasons in TB7-16268 (X (Re), 2018 CanLII 101516), a decision designated as persuasive by the Deputy Chairperson of the Refugee Appeal Division on February 27, 2019.59 They assert the RPD's credibility finding "adopted a line of reasoning that was directly contrary to the instructions provided" in the persuasive reasons.60

Having independently assessed the RPD's Reasons I reject this submission. At paragraphs 10 through 28 of the Reasons the RPD set out its concerns about similarities between the Appellants' claims and the claims in TB7-22807 before it went on to consider the principal Appellant's explanations alongside the evidence she submitted in support of her claim and the submissions of her then counsel concerning possible explanations for the similarities at paragraphs 29 through 35 of the Reasons.61

I agree that the RPD was required to decide the claim based on the evidence and not speculation, and as I have stated at paragraph 48 above the RPD's credibility finding that a third-party orchestrated both claims is speculative and wrong, as its speculation does not amount to "'sufficient reasons that clearly articulate why the claimant's explanations did not, on a balance of probabilities, demonstrate that the BoC narrative was a true representation of their story'".62

Although the RPD erred in making an insufficiently specific finding of third-party orchestration of the Appellant's claims and the claims in TB7-22807, this does not mean the RPD was required to accept either the Appellants' inadequate explanations, or the alternative possible explanations proposed by their then counsel to the RPD, including the suggestion that TB7-22807 copied the allegations in the Appellants' claims.

The Appellants point to "the timing of the claims" and assert that as they were "the first to share their story with the interpreter, Mr. Aznavehzadeh" it can reasonably be inferred that "he shared this story about the Sepah raids in Iran with the claimants in TB7-22807" who then "used it to strengthen their claim."63 As the Appellants do not support this assertion with reference to any evidence, I am not prepared to accept this assertion as, in my opinion, it is as speculative as the RPD's erroneous finding of third-party orchestration of both cases. For the same reason I reject the Appellants' submission that Mr. Aznavehzadeh's testimony in an oral hearing is necessary in order to decide their refugee claims.64

I have also considered the Appellants' submission that the XXXX Affidavit "goes directly to refuting the RPD's orchestration claim and thus is critical to the Appellants' claims."65 As I have already found the RPD erred in making a finding of third-party orchestration without reference to the XXXX Affidavit, I have examined that document to determine whether it is of any assistance in resolving any other relevant issues in this appeal.

Paragraphs five through nine inclusive of the XXXX Affidavit essentially repeat the Appellants' statements to the RPD about the circumstances in which they met Mr. XXXX, but fail to provide any additional detail or information that sheds light on the similarities between the Appellants' claims and the claims in TB7-22807. The same is true of the statements in the XXXX Affidavit concerning the adult claimants in the latter file, whom he recalls having met "around the same time that ... [he] first met ... [the principal Appellant] and her husband" even though he does "not recall exactly when".66

The affiant's further statement that he encouraged both the adult claimants in TB7-22807 "to come to the church, which they did shortly thereafter" and that they "remain member[s] of the congregation as well"67 again confirms the principal Appellant's testimony on the issue68 but fails to explain the similarities in the details between the two cases, contrary to the Appellants' submission at paragraph 81 of their memorandum-in particular, it fails to explain how the Appellants "may have been victims of a copy-cat claim".69
I therefore give the XXXX Affidavit little weight for the purpose of addressing the serious credibility issues arising from the similarities between the two cases.

To conclude on the issue of credibility, I find based on the evidence that the similarities between the two cases are a sufficient basis for drawing a serious negative inference about the principal Appellant's credibility. Common sense dictates that "the convergence of ... [the] many events" discussed in both cases "during the same narrow windows of time",70 in particular the fact that several key events in both cases including the alleged Sepah raids in Iran took place on exactly the same dates, is more than mere coincidence. The evidence of XXXX XXXX XXXX

In the Appellants' submission, the RPD's focus on the similarities between the two cases forestalled any "meaningful analysis of the Appellants' genuine conversion and Christian beliefs."71 Having read the hearing transcripts I note the RPD did question the principal Appellant about her faith and her Christian knowledge.72 According to the Reasons, the RPD found she had "a level of knowledge about Christianity that was commensurate with her attendance at church in Canada and her attendance at bible study."73

The RPD had earlier found, however, that its concerns about the principal Appellant's failure to adequately explain similarities between the Appellants' claims and the claims in TB7-22807 "seriously undermine the credibility of ... the genuineness of the claimants' [the Appellants'] religious activities in Canada."74 In my independent assessment it was open to the RPD to extend its negative inference to the Appellants' assertion that their worship in Canada was genuine, given the seriousness of the similarities and the principal Appellant's failure to adequately explain them.

According to the Appellants, however, "the best available evidence of the genuineness of the conversion [to a religious faith] may come from the claimants' pastor."75 They submit that XXXX XXXX evidence was "particularly important" because the only other reason the RPD discounted the genuineness of the Appellants' conversion was the similarity between their claims and the claims in TB7-22807.76

I am mindful that XXXX XXXX is well-placed to comment on the frequency and regularity of the Appellants' attendance at church and their pre-baptismal studies. I also acknowledge XXXX XXXX testimony that the Appellants' conversion to Christianity is "genuine and true" and that the principal Appellant's "faith and her struggle ... is accurate and faithful to what actually took place."77 The Reasons show the RPD considered XXXX XXXX XXXX testimony that the Appellants "are genuine Christians" and his testimony that "he had no reason to doubt the present claimants".78

I give little weight to the letters of XXXX XXXX, dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 201979 and XXXX XXXX XXXX 2020,80 and the note written by XXXX XXXX dated XXXX XXXX, 2019,81 all of which speak to the regularity of the Appellants' participation in Church activities. I have considered XXXX XXXX second letter dated XXXX XXXX, 2020,82 which corrects the date stated for the Appellants' entry to XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX as worshippers, and I accept the correction. I have also considered the photographs of the Appellants' participation in church activities.83 I note, however, that their participation in such activities is not in dispute and that participation in church activities does not necessarily mean that such participation is motivated by genuine Christian faith.

XXXX XXXX letters in particular purport to speak to the genuineness of the Appellants' Christian practice. For the reasons given at paragraph 65 above I am not prepared to substitute either Mr. XXXX or XXXX XXXX assessment of the genuineness of the Appellants' professed religious practice. Moreover, none of these documents addresses the main credibility issue arising from the similarities in dates between the two cases, a serious issue, not adequately explained, that has a severe deleterious impact on the Appellants' credibility.

In my assessment paragraphs 61 to 63 inclusive of the Appellants' written submissions in their Memorandum essentially invite me to substitute XXXX XXXX assessment-and by analogy I include the assessments of XXXX XXXX and Mr. XXXX-of the genuineness of the Appellants' conversion to Christianity for the RPD's finding that their conversion was not genuine. I decline to do so: in assessing the genuineness of the Appellants' conversion I am required to consider and weigh XXXX XXXX testimony alongside all the other evidence before me, in light of my finding that the principal Appellant's credibility is seriously undermined by her failure to explain why many key elements of her claim are so similar to those in the claims in TB7-22807.
Having done so, I find the Appellants' evidence fails to establish that the motives for their conversion to Christianity in Canada were genuine. The Appellants' sur place claim

The Federal Court of Canada's reasons for judgment in Ejtehadian state: In assessing the Applicant's risks of return, in the context of a sur-place claim, it is necessary to consider the credible evidence of his activities while in Canada, independently from his motives for conversion. Even if the Applicant's motives for conversion are not genuine, as found by the IRB [Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada] here, the consequential imputation of apostasy to the Applicant by the authorities in Iran may nonetheless be sufficient to bring him within the scope of the convention definition.84

The RPD found the Appellants did not have a sur place claim, as there was "no evidence" their "religious activities would come to the attention of Iranian authorities in such a way that they would cause the ... [Appellants] to face a serious possibility of persecution in Iran."85 The Appellants submit, in response, that there was some documentary evidence in the NDP that supported their sur place claim, and referred to two items that discuss the targeting of failed refugee claimants upon their return to Iran and the "monitoring of activities outside of Iran" by agents of that country's government.86

Simply disclosing general documentary evidence that touches upon the treatment of failed refugee claimants and Christians in Iran, however, is insufficient to ground a sur place claim when that evidence fails to disclose any connection with the Appellants in Canada.

Nor have the Appellants established with clear and convincing evidence that their religious activities in Canada have been brought to the attention of authorities in Iran, or would be in the future.87 Before the RPD the Appellants' then counsel relied on the Federal Court's reasons for judgment in Sheikh in arguing that the relevant question for the panel was not the likelihood authorities in Iran would learn of the Appellants' conversion to Christianity, but rather "what objectively will happen if the situation becomes known".88

However, the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees' Handbook on Procedures and Criteria for Determining Refugee Status under the 1951 Convention and the 1967 Protocol relating to the Status of Refugees provides that those determining refugee status should consider whether a claimant's activities in the country of residence "may have come to the notice of the authorities of the person's country of origin" in addition to how those activities would be viewed by those authorities.89

I acknowledge that if the principal Appellant's conversion to Christianity were to come to the attention of the authorities in Iran she would be a target of persecution disguised as prosecution under criminal laws in that country that characterize her activities as tantamount to apostasy. However the Appellants also bear the onus of establishing with clear and convincing evidence how her activities in Iran might have come to the attention of that country's authorities, beyond merely pointing to country conditions documents in the NDP.

In my independent assessment, the fact the Appellants belong to a Protestant Christian church in Canada and engage in its activities, including religious practice, does not amount to proof that their activities may have come to the attention of authorities in Iran, such that they would face persecution in Iran upon returning to that country, notwithstanding its apostasy laws.
As no such evidence was before the RPD it did not err in finding the Appellants failed to establish they had a sur place claim.

I also find the Appellants have not disclosed any such evidence in this appeal. I have examined the documents in their four Refugee Appeal Division Rules rule 29 application records and none of them, including the letter from the Executive Director of the Flemingdon Park Ministry,90 suggests that the Appellants' activities in Canada have or would come to the attention of authorities in Iran who would punish them for their perceived conversion.
I therefore find the Appellants do not have a sur place claim.

I also reject as specious the Appellants' submission91 that the RPD applied the wrong standard of proof in assessing the Appellants' sur place claim. The submission that the RPD's use of the word "would" at paragraph 41 of the Reasons raises the standard of proof applicable to the Appellants' claims above the "more than a mere possibility" threshold appears to confuse the requirement that a claimant establish the facts of his or her case on a balance of probabilities (the standard of proof) with the distinct requirement that a claimant show that those facts meet the legal test for protection under section 96 of the IRPA (whether a claimant faces a serious possibility of persecution).92

In this case the RPD stated the correct standard of proof near the start of the Reasons.93 Based on my independent assessment of the Appellant's credibility, I find the RPD did not err in finding the Appellants failed to establish the factual (evidentiary) basis of their allegation that their activities in Canada might draw the attention of authorities in Iran, an allegation on which their sur place claim relied. The minor Appellant

The Appellants submit the RPD erred by failing to independently assess the genuineness of the minor Appellant XXXX conversion to Christianity. They submit that "[t]he documentary evidence and the pastor's testimony supported a finding that Sam's conversion was genuine"94 and the RPD should not have relied "solely on its credibility findings concerning [the principal Appellant]" to characterize her son's conversion as not genuine.95

In my independent assessment, there was no reason for the RPD to assess his claim independently because he did not articulate an independent claim. XXXX was ten years old at the time of the hearing, and relied on the testimony and other evidence disclosed by his mother and the witness's testimony. In light of this, the fact that some evidence refers to or identifies XXXX distinctly or by name does not ground a finding that his claim warranted assessment independently of his mother's claim. Summary

In light of the foregoing, I find that despite the errors in certain of the RPD's adverse credibility findings, the panel did not err in its overall determination that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.
The appeal is dismissed.

I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD, for other reasons, that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection, pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the IRPA.
